title: Shazam Algorithm & Text Deduplication Landscape Synthesis
summary: Comprehensive research synthesizing Shazam's landmark-pair audio fingerprinting mechanism, comparing it to existing text deduplication methods (MinHash, Winnowing, SimHash, RETSim), and documenting key technical gaps and design decisions required to adapt audio landmark pairing to text near-duplicate detection for structural edits. The investigation maps audio concepts (spectral peaks, frequency identity, relative time-delta) to text equivalents (TF-IDF landmarks, n-gram types, position-delta offsets) while identifying critical challenges (n-gram brittleness vs audio peak robustness, boilerplate collision risk, large-scale reordering vulnerability). The landmark-pair approach shows theoretical promise for ~10pp recall improvement on structural edits via offset-consistency matching, but success is contingent on sparse boilerplate density, limited paraphrase edits, and robust parameter tuning.
answer:
## Shazam's Audio Fingerprinting Algorithm: Core Mechanism

Shazam (2003) is an industrial-strength audio search engine deployed commercially that identifies songs from brief, noisy samples (15 seconds) captured through cellphone microphones [1]. The algorithm's core innovation is **combinatorial peak pairing with relative time offsets**, achieving massive speedup and robustness through offset-consistency matching rather than individual landmark comparison [1]. Each hash encodes (frequency₁, frequency₂, time_delta) into a compact 32-bit token [1]. This peak-pairing strategy achieves two critical properties: (a) ~10,000× speedup over single-point matching because pair specificity is 1,000,000× higher (30 bits information vs 10 bits) [1], and (b) robustness via offset-consistency voting—spurious hash collisions are unlikely to have consistent offsets across multiple matches, providing inherent noise resistance [1].

## Spectrogram Generation & Peak Detection

Audio is converted to a spectrogram (3D time-frequency-energy matrix) via Fast Fourier Transform on overlapping 4-32ms time windows [2]. The frequency resolution is approximately 40 Hz spacing using standard music sampling rates (22.05 kHz or 44.1 kHz) [2, 3]. Spectral peaks are identified as time-frequency points with higher energy than neighbors, selected for both amplitude (highest peaks survive distortion) and density (uniform coverage across spectrogram) [1]. This results in a sparse constellation map of (frequency, time) coordinates that resembles a star field [1]. The spectrogram approach is fundamentally robust because spectral peaks survive noise, GSM codec compression, and EQ filtering—properties that make them ideal fingerprints for captured mobile audio [1]. Peak survival probability under noise is high because peaks remain distinct above noise floor and maintain position invariance [1].

## Combinatorial Peak Pairing Strategy

The core innovation pairs spectrogram peaks to form hash tokens [1]. For each detected peak serving as an ANCHOR POINT, a forward-looking TARGET ZONE is defined (e.g., 0-30ms ahead) [1]. A fan-out factor F (typically F=10) limits pairing to control combinatorial explosion [1]. For each (anchor, target) pair, three components are extracted: (frequency₁, frequency₂, time_delta) where time_delta = target_time - anchor_time [1]. These are combined into a single 32-bit hash token with typical encoding: 10 bits per frequency + 10 bits time difference + 2-12 bits quantization [1]. Critical design decision: use RELATIVE time-delta (not absolute time) to achieve translation-invariance—the same audio sample matches at any position in database track [1]. Hash survivability under noise follows: probability ~p² (both peaks must survive), but this is offset by generating F times more hashes per anchor, yielding overall survival ~p*[1-(1-p)^F], which for F>10 and p>0.1 remains close to p [1].

## Database Indexing & Query Matching

All hashes from database tracks are pre-computed and stored in an inverted index: hash_value → [(track_id, time_offset), ...] [1]. Typical storage: 64-bit structs with 32-bit hash + 32-bit time offset + track ID [1]. For query, the same fingerprinting algorithm generates hashes from sample audio. Each query hash is looked up in database index; matching (track_id, offset) tuples are collected [1]. The key insight: if query correctly matches database track, all matching hashes should have nearly IDENTICAL time offsets (time_delta_db - time_delta_query ≈ constant) [1]. Time-offset bins are scanned for high agreement; bins with many consistent votes indicate correct match; spurious matches have random offsets [1]. This offset-consistency filtering provides robustness without requiring high individual hash survival [1]. Query performance achieves sub-millisecond times on massive databases due to hash indexing [1].

## Text Deduplication Methods: Comparative Landscape

### MinHash + LSH (Broder 1997, Manku et al. 2007)

MinHash estimates Jaccard similarity between documents via k-gram shingles and random hash minima [4, 5]. Locality-Sensitive Hashing with banding provides sub-linear candidate retrieval; typical deployment uses 100-1000 hash functions, 10-20 bands, similarity threshold 0.8-0.95 [4, 6]. Strengths: proven at massive scale (Google web crawler, HuggingFace datasets, LLM training pipelines), fast O(1) comparison post-sketch, no training required [5, 6]. Critical weakness: global statistic sensitive to structural additions. If passage is 100 shingles and 500 surrounding tokens added, Jaccard = 100/(100+500) = 0.17, well below typical 0.8 threshold, causing detection failure [4, 7]. Individual shingles lack positional structure; sparse fingerprints on short/low-entropy text; hash-busting attacks possible [6].

### Winnowing (Schleimer et al. 2003)

Winnowing selects minimum hash in sliding windows of k-gram hashes to produce compact fingerprints [8]. Lightweight approach deployed in MOSS plagiarism detector [8]. Strengths: fast single-pass computation (one pass over document), local robustness to paragraph reordering within windows [8, 9]. Weaknesses: individual landmarks lack positional offset information; insertion/deletion at window boundaries shifts which hash is selected, causing recall loss; no pairing mechanism for redundancy [8, 9]. Window size represents tradeoff: small windows → sparse fingerprint sensitive to local edits; large windows → dense fingerprint with computational cost [9].

### SimHash (Charikar 2002)

SimHash projects TF-IDF vector onto random hyperplanes, yielding 64-128 bit hash; similar documents have small Hamming distance [10, 11]. Deployed by Google since 2006 for web-scale near-duplicate detection of billions of pages [10]. Strengths: fast bit operations for similarity comparison, single dense vector representation [11]. Critical weaknesses: loses local structure in global vector representation; insensitive to which part of document changed; TF-IDF estimates unreliable for domain-specific text; random hyperplane introduces variance [11]. Global statistic cannot distinguish passages embedded in different contexts [11].

### RETSim (Zhang et al. 2023)

RETSim is a neural embedding model (536k parameters) fine-tuned on typo-augmented corpus using metric learning for character-level robustness [12]. Introduces W4NT3D benchmark (Wiki-40B 4dversarial Near-T3xt Dataset) for multilingual adversarial near-duplicates [12]. Achieves state-of-the-art on typo-laden text (2024 ICLR); ~5-15pp F1 improvement over MinHash on adversarial tasks with 20-30% typo rates [12]. Critical weaknesses: requires training on typo-augmented corpus (violates training-free constraint if constraint exists), 46× slower than MinHash on CPU for inference [12], less interpretable than discrete hash tokens [12], model deployment cost [12].

## Audio-to-Text Concept Mapping

Shazam's core concepts map to text as follows [1, 2, 3]:

**Spectrogram (time-frequency energy)** → **TF-IDF surface** (position × n-gram saliency matrix). Spectrogram shows energy distribution across frequencies over time; TF-IDF matrix shows importance of n-grams at different positions [2, 13].

**Spectral peak (high energy in narrow frequency band)** → **Local TF-IDF maximum** (high-saliency n-gram at specific position). Audio peak is high energy at specific time-frequency; text landmark is high-saliency n-gram at specific position [2, 3, 13].

**Frequency identity** → **N-gram type** (character or word sequence). Audio frequency (e.g., 440 Hz) is intrinsic feature; text n-gram identity (e.g., 'ing' or 'the') is intrinsic feature [2, 13].

**Time position** → **Character/word position** in document. Audio sample position (milliseconds); text position (character or word index) [2, 13].

**Time-delta (relative offset between peaks)** → **Position-delta** (offset between n-gram positions). Shazam uses relative time (not absolute) for translation-invariance; text uses relative position for position-invariance [1, 2, 13].

**Hash(freq₁, freq₂, delta_t)** → **Hash(ngram₁, ngram₂, delta_pos)** (32-bit tokens). Both encode pair identity + relative offset [1, 13].

### Critical Gaps in Audio-to-Text Mapping

**Gap 1—Saliency Definition**: Spectral energy is physically well-defined (power in frequency band); TF-IDF is statistical and corpus-dependent, unreliable for domain-specific text or short passages [2, 13]. **Gap 2—Invariance**: Spectral peaks survive noise predictably (peaks remain peaks above noise floor); n-grams do NOT survive lexical changes (synonyms, typos, paraphrase destroy n-gram identity), making text landmarks fundamentally noisier [2, 12, 13]. **Gap 3—Structure**: Audio fingerprinting is signal-agnostic; text deduplication must handle both syntactic (spacing, case, punctuation) and semantic changes (word order, synonymy) [13]. **Gap 4—Sparse Landmarks**: Boilerplate text generates sparse landmarks creating false negatives; dense text may generate spurious landmark collision creating false positives [13]. **Gap 5—Pairing Assumption**: Shazam assumes relative peak distances invariant under common transformations (noise, EQ); large-scale reordering (paragraph shuffling) breaks positional offset assumptions [13].

## Robustness to Structural Edits: Analysis

### Insertion (Surrounding Text Added)
MinHash degrades severely: if passage is 100 shingles and 500 tokens added before/after, Jaccard = 100/(100+500) = 0.17, well below typical 0.8 threshold [7]. Detection fails completely [13]. Landmark pairs show PARTIAL SURVIVAL: internal pairs (not spanning insertion boundaries) preserve unchanged relative offsets; pairs spanning insertion boundaries are affected but represent small fraction of fingerprint [13]. Offset-consistency matching filters spurious collisions from added text [1, 13].

### Deletion (Paragraphs Removed)
MinHash scores halved if 50% deleted (Jaccard = 0.5), below threshold [13]. Winnowing loses landmarks at deletion boundaries [13]. Landmark pairs: pairs entirely before/after deleted section survive with unchanged relative offsets; pairs spanning deletion have altered deltas [13]. Survival proportional to deletion location relative to landmark positions [13].

### Embedding (Passage in Larger Document)
If passage is 100 tokens embedded in 1100-token document with dissimilar boilerplate, Jaccard ≈ 0.09 [13]. Detection fails [13]. Landmark pairs: if boilerplate is sparse (low n-gram density), sparse spurious landmarks generated by boilerplate → low false-positive risk [13]. If boilerplate is dense (high n-gram density), many spurious landmark pairs created in boilerplate region → collision risk [13]. Offset consistency can filter coincidental collisions but dense boilerplate represents empirical risk [13].

## Parameter Design Space for Text Adaptation

### N-gram Size
Character n-grams (5-8 chars): robust to word boundary ambiguity, language-agnostic, handles punctuation naturally; tradeoff is large vocabulary (~12M possible 5-grams) [13]. Word n-grams (1-3 words): capture semantic content, smaller vocabulary (~10k-100k); tradeoff is tokenization-dependency, case-sensitivity [13]. **Recommendation**: Start with 5-8 character n-grams as middle ground balancing distinctiveness and density [13].

### Lookahead Window W (Target Zone Size)
Shazam uses 30-50ms forward time window for pairing target peaks to anchor [1]. Text equivalent: 20-50 token lookahead (balances fine-grained local structure vs noise from distant n-grams) [13]. Smaller W → sparse pairs, fine resolution, low noise; Larger W → dense pairs, captures longer structure, more noise [13].

### Landmark Density Threshold
Shazam selects peaks by density criterion ensuring uniform coverage [1]. Text equivalent: keep top 10-15% n-grams by TF-IDF [13]. High threshold (top 5%) → sparse fingerprint, fast computation, risk of missing landmarks in low-variance passages [13]. Low threshold (top 20%) → denser fingerprint, more robust, increased noise and computation [13].

### TF-IDF Context Window
100-200 tokens around each position for local TF-IDF computation (balances robust IDF estimates vs spatial resolution) [13]. Smaller window → unreliable IDF on sparse samples; Larger window → includes unrelated context reducing locality [13].

### Hash Output Size & Quantization
32-bit tokens (Shazam standard) with quantization of position-delta to reduce sensitivity to small positional shifts (e.g., round to nearest 5 tokens) [1, 13]. Quantization tradeoff: coarser → more robust to small edits but less precise; finer → more precise but fragile [13].

## Inverted Indexing & Lookup Strategy

### Simple Inverted Index
Structure: hash_value → [(passage_id, time_offset), ...] [13]. For query: generate all landmark-pair hashes, look up each hash in index, collect candidates, rank by match count [13]. Query complexity: O(H * L) where H = # hashes in query, L = average # candidates per hash; with good hash function, L ~ 1-10 [13]. Space: O(D * H_avg) where D = # passages, H_avg = avg hashes per passage [13]. Advantages: simple, deterministic, no tuning parameters [13]. Disadvantages: no tunable precision-recall tradeoff; hash collisions create false positives (but multiple consistent matches filter these) [13].

### Banded LSH Alternative
Motivation: simple index doesn't tune precision vs recall; LSH banding provides tunable threshold [13]. Algorithm: divide landmark-pair hash sketch into B bands of r hashes each; for each band, hash to bucket; passage is candidate if it appears in ANY bucket (collision in any band) [13]. Threshold formula: T ≈ 1 - (1/B)^(1/r); higher B → higher T (more selective, higher precision, lower recall) [13]. Example: B=10, r=10 → T≈0.63 [13]. Recommendation: implement simple index for hypothesis testing (iteration 1); only optimize to LSH if precision-recall tuning critical (iteration 2) [13].

## Benchmark & Evaluation Strategy

### PAN-PC-11 (Standard Plagiarism Corpus)
26.9k documents, 61k plagiarism cases covering multiple obfuscation types (copy+paste, automatic paraphrasing, minor changes) [14]. Baseline benchmark; landmark pairs should match or exceed MinHash on standard scenarios [14].

### Synthetic Structural-Edit Corpus
500 Wikipedia passages × 5 variants each = 2,500 (passage, edit) pairs [13]. Variant types: INSERTION (add 200-500 tokens boilerplate before/after), DELETION (remove middle 20-30%), EMBEDDING (place in 2000-token document with dissimilar context), COMBINED (multiple edits) [13]. Ground truth: passage_id and variant_id pairs are duplicates [13].

### W4NT3D Benchmark (Adversarial)
Wiki-40B with systematic typos and character edits; multilingual coverage [12]. Adversarial benchmark for robustness; provides hard negatives (near-duplicates with high typo rates) [12].

### Evaluation Metrics
Precision-recall curves (vary threshold T via LSH banding); F1 score as primary metric; area under PR curve [13]. Per-benchmark results: separate curves for each benchmark to isolate strengths (PAN-PC-11) vs weaknesses (structural edits) [13].

### Ablation Studies
(1) With/without positional offset matching: isolates value of offset consistency [13]. (2) Landmark density k: vary top-k% by TF-IDF, measure recall@precision vs k [13]. (3) Lookahead window W: vary 5-100 tokens, measure sensitivity [13]. (4) Hash quantization: with/without position-delta quantization, measure robustness [13].

### Success Criteria
~10pp recall improvement over MinHash at precision ≥0.90 on synthetic structural-edit corpus [13]; lookup latency ≤10ms per query on 1M-passage corpus (sub-linear scaling) [13]; fingerprint sparsity within 2× of MinHash (memory-efficient) [13].

### Failure Conditions
Only ~5pp improvement or less → hypothesis refuted [13]. Lookup 10× slower than MinHash LSH → impractical despite accuracy [13]. Fingerprints 5× larger than MinHash → memory bloat outweighs gains [13].

## Critical Design Decisions for Iteration 2

### Decision 1: N-gram Type (Character vs Word)
Tradeoff: character 5-8-grams (training-free, handles diverse text, large vocabulary) vs word n-grams (semantic content, smaller vocabulary, tokenization-dependent). **Recommendation**: Start with 5-8 character n-grams to isolate pairing mechanism as variable; adapt vocabulary only if landmark density too sparse [13].

### Decision 2: Indexing Approach (Simple vs LSH Banding)
Tradeoff: simple inverted index (easier implementation, deterministic, no tuning) vs LSH banding (tunable precision-recall, proven at scale). **Recommendation**: Implement simple index for iteration 1; hypothesis testing doesn't require LSH; only optimize to banding if precision-recall tuning is load-bearing (iteration 2+) [13].

### Decision 3: Saliency Selection (Fixed TF-IDF vs Learned)
Tradeoff: fixed TF-IDF (training-free, interpretable, aligns with Shazam's fixed spectral energy concept) vs learned neural saliency (adaptive, requires training, violates training-free constraint). **Recommendation**: Fixed TF-IDF to isolate pairing mechanism as load-bearing variable; learned saliency deferred to iteration 3+ if marginal gains warrant training cost [13].

## Synthesis: Value Proposition of Landmark-Pair Approach

Shazam's core innovation—combinatorial peak pairing with relative time offsets—provides robustness via offset-consistency matching (multiple hashes voting for same offset = strong signal) rather than global statistics [1]. MinHash relies on global Jaccard (diluted by additions), Winnowing on individual landmarks (no positional structure), SimHash on dense vectors (loses locality), RETSim on learned embeddings (requires training) [4, 8, 10, 12]. Landmark pairs preserve structure under insertion/deletion at passage boundaries because internal relative offsets unchanged [13]. However, theoretical advantage assumes: (a) sparse boilerplate (low spurious landmark collision rate), (b) limited paraphrase edits (n-gram identity preserved under synonym substitution), (c) no large-scale reordering (paragraph shuffling breaks offset assumptions) [13]. Predicted ~10pp recall improvement is plausible if these assumptions hold, but success is empirically contingent on corpus characteristics and parameter tuning [13].

## Confidence Assessment

**Very High (95%+)**: Shazam algorithm mechanics, text dedup methods documented in academic literature and production deployments [1, 4, 8, 10, 12]. **High (85%+)**: Text dedup method comparisons, strengths/weaknesses empirically validated [4, 6, 7, 8, 12]. **Moderate (70%+)**: Audio-to-text concept mapping conceptually sound but untested in practice; gaps identified are plausible but lack empirical validation [2, 13]. **Moderate (65%)**: Structural edit robustness argument theoretically justified but depends on empirical corpus characteristics [13]. **Low-Moderate (45%)**: Success prediction of ~10pp improvement heavily contingent on boilerplate density distribution and n-gram collision rates; empirical study required [13].

follow_up_questions: How does landmark pair density scale with corpus characteristics? Boilerplate-heavy text (technical documentation, news templates) generates sparse landmarks while highly-varied text (literature, diverse articles) generates dense landmarks. What is the typical landmark density distribution across real-world corpora, and does it critically affect false-positive collision probability?

How sensitive is offset-consistency matching to quantization granularity? Fine-grained position offsets (exact token positions) vs coarse quantization (5-10 token buckets) represent different robustness-specificity tradeoffs; what quantization granularity optimizes both recall on structural edits and precision against false positives?

What is the collision probability bound for landmark pairs in 32-bit hash space at scale? With billions of passages each generating thousands of landmark pairs, expected false-positive rate depends on hash space size and n-gram vocabulary collision rate—can collision probability be analytically bounded or must it be empirically measured on real corpora?
